extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/logic; readers interested in the theory of causation and scientific explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating causal claims and theories of causation in philosophy and science: what counts as a cause, tests to distinguish real causation from mere concomitance, and how to judge appeals to volition or other metaphysical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation as a set of antecedents connected by invariable and unconditional sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: “That set, or those sets, of antecedents are its cause.” The cause of a phenomenon is the assemblage (one or more sets) of antecedent conditions that are connected to the phenomenon by invariable and unconditional sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate causal claims by identifying the antecedent conditions that habitually and unconditionally precede the phenomenon. Examples: to produce a bonfire one needs fuel, air, a spark (collocations) and chemical action (a force). Emphasizes regularity (invariable sequence) rather than metaphysical labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation: change can only be produced by change
rubrics_metrics.description: “The law of causation is, that change can only be produced by change.” A genuine cause must include at least one changing antecedent (a force), not only stationary collocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging causes, check that among the antecedents there is an active or changing element (force) rather than only static conditions. Static collocations alone do not suffice unless paired with an active antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish two elements in the cause: presence of a force and collocation/position of objects
rubrics_metrics.description: We must distinguish in the assemblage of conditions which constitutes the Cause of a phenomenon, two elements: one, the presence of a force; the other, the collocation or position of objects which is required in order that the force may undergo the particular transmutation which constitutes the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both whether an appropriate force is present and whether the physical arrangement (collocation) allows that force to produce the particular effect. Example: grinding corn requires both the collocation of the mill parts and a driving force (water, wind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure or transfer of energy as a test distinguishing causation from mere concomitance
rubrics_metrics.description: Admit, as one of the tests for distinguishing causation from mere concomitance, the expenditure or transfer of energy: if the effect consists in putting matter in motion, then any object which has lost motion has contributed to the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical bookkeeping—loss/gain of motion or energy—to identify causal contributors when appropriate. If an antecedent’s motion/energy is expended in producing the effect, that antecedent is a genuine causal contributor rather than a mere concomitant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Force as Potentiality of Motion (not necessarily actual motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true definition of Force must be, not motion, but Potentiality of Motion; what the doctrine amounts to is that the possibilities of motion are limited to a definite quantity and that actual motion is a draft upon this stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing causal power to objects, recognize that the relevant property may be a potentiality (capacity to produce motion under appropriate collocation) rather than actual present motion. This affects how one traces causes under conservation principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require external/empirical evidence rather than subjective conceivability for positing efficient causes (critique of volition-as-cause)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not substitute subjective feelings of conceivability for external evidence when deciding between causal theories; proponents who appeal to a priori consciousness of volition as proof of its universal causal efficacy fail to provide positive evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject arguments that infer real causal status solely from their apparent intelligibility or from internal feelings (e.g., ‘consciousness of effort’). Demand empirical or independent grounds before accepting that volition (or any proposed cause) is the efficient cause of phenomena beyond the familiar cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of the familiarity/assimilation bias when judging what is conceivable as a cause
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a spontaneous tendency of the intellect to assimilate unfamiliar causal relations to familiar voluntary acts; what appears 'natural' or 'conceivable' is often only what is familiar to the thinker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cognitive bias: do not accept as intrinsically explanatory those causal hypotheses that only feel intelligible because they resemble the thinker’s familiar cases. Historical and comparative evidence may reveal alternative ‘intelligible’ physical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from a single familiar instance to universal causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fallacious to infer that because volition is the efficient cause of our bodily motions, it must be the direct cause of all phenomena; generalizations from a single kind of instance require resemblance in relevant respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate generalizations by checking similarity of laws and manifestations: only generalize when other cases manifest the same sorts of indicators (e.g., similar phenomena, similar lawful regularities), not merely because of shared status as 'instances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and linguistic considerations as evidence about origins of causal belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of languages and the history of philosophical belief show how early minds attributed agency to natural objects; this background explains why some causal notions (like volitional causation) persist and should inform our evaluation of such theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical and linguistic facts as auxiliary evidence to diagnose whether a causal theory is rooted in instinctive or culturally contingent tendencies rather than in independent empirical support. Treat such evidence as cautions against accepting theories grounded mainly in instinctive familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a physical theory reinterprets phenomena (e.g., Conservation of Force), check whether it requires changes in conception of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Conservation theory (reducing force to motion) suggests reinterpreting what we call 'force' as potential motion; but this does not necessarily require changing the logical principle of causation—causes remain antecedent sets connected by sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting new scientific doctrines that reinterpret causal language, ensure you translate the old causal attributions into the new conceptual vocabulary without losing the logical/testable criteria for causation (antecedence, regularity, transfer of energy, collocation).
